title: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
hook: the lord who raises and tends every world, not just yours

segments.voice: Yesterday: alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God. Today it turns out to be the first word of a verse you say in every prayer. Day twelve.

On day two you heard al-Fatiha whole, all seven verses in one go. For the next five days it slows down: one verse at a time, inside words you may have said a thousand times. Verse two begins with yesterday's word. Praise be to God. Then it points that praise somewhere enormous. Not at your day. At every world there is.
screen: `AL-FATIHA, SLOWED DOWN.` → `VERSE TWO: ALHAMDULILLAH.` → `EVERY WORLD THERE IS.`

segments.voice: Verse two: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” In Arabic, al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin. The first half is yesterday's word. The new word is Rabb. English says Lord, which is right, but thin. Rabb is the one who owns and the one who looks after. Commentators explain it with the picture of raising something: bringing a child, or a seedling, along step by step until it's grown. So a rabb isn't a distant owner with paperwork. It's the one who feeds, shelters and brings you up. Then al-'alamin: the worlds. Not the world: the worlds, plural. Commentators have listed people, angels, animals, every kind of created thing. The ant colony under the sidewalk. The deep sea. The inside of a stranger's life on the train. All of it, the verse says, is being raised and tended by one Rabb. And remember the conversation from day two. At this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me. The praise isn't said into empty air. It's heard, and answered.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE.` · `RABB — THE ONE WHO RAISES.` · `AL-'ALAMIN — THE WORLDS, PLURAL.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. First, your own world: one thing in it that's being looked after, even today. Stay with it. Then a world that isn't yours: a bird, a stranger, a field somewhere you'll never see. Then hold both at once. If you want, the Arabic can ride out on a breath: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin.
Rabb. Lord: the one who owns, raises and looks after, here the Lord of all the worlds. Twelfth word.
Your line: every world is tended. Yours, and every one you'll never see. Day twelve.

howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and many say alhamdulillah, its opening word, many times a day. Rabb is also the word Muslims use in many personal prayers, often as Rabbi, my Lord, or Rabbana, our Lord.

fork.setup: someone praying says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. in the hadith qudsi from day two, what happens next?
options: nothing: prayer is a one-way message.
God answers: My servant has praised Me.
fork.reveal: the hadith describes al-Fatiha as a conversation. at this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me.

original.note: Arabic: lord, master, the one who raises and looks after. in al-Fatiha: rabbi l-'alamin, Lord of the Worlds.

trapdoor: what you thought: "Lord" — a title, like a king's.
what it means: the one who owns and looks after, raising every world along.
what a scholar hears: commentators gloss rabb with tarbiya, bringing a thing gradually to completion; al-'alamin, plural of 'alam, is read as every class of creation.

notes: Moved: old day 7 → day 12. The old hook was week one's look-back; it's rewritten to open the verse-by-verse walk (days 12–16), which now follows day two's whole-surah lesson and day eleven's alhamdulillah. Lightened: Muslim no longer named in the spoken text, 'two verses down, five to go' cut, no homework in the carry, the practice is the 45-second sit.

Rabb explained through tarbiya (raising step by step to completion) follows classical commentators such as al-Baydawi; lexicographers differ on whether tarbiya shares rabb's root. The script says 'commentators explain it with the picture of raising'; confirm.
Al-'alamin as every class of creation (people, angels, animals, jinn): a common tafsir reading among several. Confirm.
Sahih Muslim 395 (hadith qudsi, 'I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant') cited from memory; the script paraphrases. Please confirm the number.
